chapter: Later career and The Benny Goodman Story
title: Learning how movies are made and respect for actors
summary: Wilson describes how each short scene was shot several times from different camera angles and why he came to respect professional actors.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: No, I don't remember that either.

No. It was quite an experience making that movie. I got to respect actors more. Before I worked in that movie ... well, I had worked in movies before, but that was just doing little bits in a nightclub scene, without having to say any words, but in the Goodman story, I had quite a few lines to say, and you know, things that are very easy for you to do when you're sitting in the living room -- but when the clock is ticking to 4,3,2, 1, 'talk' -- and do it like that, then everything becomes very difficult.

Even like where you're gonna put your hand, or you have to walk over and sit down in the chair or walk to a certain point and start talking -- it all becomes very complex and you can get stiff and look awkward, and the director says, cut, and do it again -- have to keep going over it until you get a take that he is satisfied with.

And most every situation on the screen, they photograph it in little bits of maybe 5 to 10 seconds. So you can imagine the amount of work that goes into a movie that runs an hour and a half or so, when it's photographed in five-second bits. And those five seconds are done over and over and over again, and then you move on to the next step. But rarely is a scene over 10 or 15 seconds. Every
scene is done with at least three different ... (CUT)
What were you saying before we cut?
Well, each scene is done at least three times from three different camera angles.

For instance, we're talking like this, say the scene says to say, 'Hello, Milt' and you say 'Hello, Teddy!' and then one camera will photograph you saying hello to me, and then you'll be listening to me saying 'Hello, Milt' and you'll be listening to me, and then the other camera will photograph on my face and we go through the whole thing again, and then there is an overall camera that has the two of us both in the picture so that the 'Hello, Milt, Hello, Teddy' is done at least three times.

And then each one has to be done to the director's satisfaction, because he knows when it's done properly and not stiff. That it's natural, the acting part of it. But it takes a long time to make a good movie.

And you can see the professionals out there in action, like people like Donna Reed, they act like, when we go and play a piece of music, you know, like well, now we're gonna play 'Sunny Side of the Street' -- well, we know
"Sunny Side of the Street" and we'll play it. But those people, when it comes time to act, they go into the character and they act just like we play music.

That's why I say I have a lot of respect for real actors, because they are pros, they can just do it. You know? They just say it like it's supposed to be said, and the character they are portraying projects itself to the viewer.
